analysis.one_liner: Restores patients' right to sue medical device makers in state court for defective devices.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 71 cosponsors, was sent to a House committee and never received a vote before the 2008 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2008 the Supreme Court ruled that FDA approval of a medical device shields the manufacturer from most injury lawsuits under state law. This bill would change federal law to say that FDA approval does not block state lawsuits over defective devices, restoring patients' ability to sue device makers in state courts. It would also apply to lawsuits already in progress. The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients injured by defective medical devices, and their families, who would regain the ability to seek damages in state courts. State attorneys general and consumer advocates would also regain a tool for holding device makers accountable.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act stating that the federal preemption rules for medical devices 'shall not be construed to modify or otherwise affect any action for damages or the liability of any person under the law of any State,' restoring state-court injury lawsuits against device makers.

It would apply to any civil action pending or filed after enactment, and would take effect as if it had been part of the Medical Device Amendments of 1976, so patients with existing claims would benefit, not only future ones.

analysis.who_pays: Medical device manufacturers, who would face jury trials and damage awards in state courts for devices the FDA approved, and whose insurers would bear higher litigation and liability costs. Some of that cost could be passed to hospitals and patients through higher device prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medical device manufacturers and their insurers

drawbacks.text: Device makers and their industry group argue that a uniform federal standard is what the FDA approval system was designed to provide, and that letting state juries effectively set different safety requirements for the same approved device could discourage innovation and delay new devices from reaching patients.

Applying the change to lawsuits already pending or filed, rather than only future cases, would expose manufacturers to retroactive liability for conduct that occurred when federal law appeared to shield them, and litigation costs could contribute to higher device prices for hospitals and patients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefit is direct: the right to hold a manufacturer accountable in court when an approved device injures them, instead of being left with no remedy because of FDA approval. The costs are real but diffuse — manufacturers face litigation risk and some price pressure, and manufacturers argue that a patchwork of state judgments could complicate a system built on one federal approval standard. On balance, the bill shifts power from manufacturers back to injured patients and state courts.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2008, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, and sat there until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 26, 2008, by Rep. Frank Pallone with 60 original cosponsors listed on the floor, and was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to its Subcommittee on Health.
The bill attracted 71 cosponsors in total — 66 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but no further action was ever taken on it.
It was still pending in subcommittee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and bills that are not passed by the end of a Congress die and must be reintroduced from scratch.

The bill was a response to the Supreme Court's February 2008 decision in Riegel v. Medtronic, which held that FDA premarket approval of a medical device preempts most state-law injury claims, leaving patients injured by approved devices with no damages remedy.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical device manufacturers are better off: by never getting a vote, the bill preserved the liability shield from FDA preemption that the Supreme Court had recognized, leaving injured patients without state-court remedies. House members face no recorded vote on the issue.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-NJ), bill sponsor and chair of the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 60 original cosponsors.

for.name: 71 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad House support.

for.name: Medical device plaintiffs' attorneys and consumer advocates
for.role: Supporters of restoring state-court liability for device injuries
for.what_they_did: Publicly supported legislation to overturn the effect of the Riegel v. Medtronic preemption ruling.

against.name: Rep. John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled action on the bill, which died in the Health Subcommittee.

against.name: Medical device industry
against.role: Manufacturers of FDA-approved medical devices (including AdvaMed, the industry trade group)
against.what_they_did: Opposed stripping the preemption shield and supported the Riegel ruling that FDA approval blocks state injury lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 71 cosponsors included 66 Democrats and only 5 Republicans, so support skewed heavily Democratic, though no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill would remove the legal shield created by FDA preemption, exposing makers of approved devices to state-court injury lawsuits and damage awards. Their interest in keeping that shield runs directly against injured patients' ability to sue.
Device makers' liability insurers would face more claims and higher payouts if state lawsuits were restored, and those costs could partly flow through to device prices.
